abstract: A common measure of the quality of a voting rule is the social welfare of the alternatives it elects. Prior work shows that, when voter utilities are drawn from a neutral distribution, expected utilitarian welfare is maximized by a positional scoring rule. We extend this approach to the power mean family of welfare functions, which includes utilitarian, Nash, and egalitarian welfare as special cases. We show that, across the power mean family, a deterministic positional scoring rule (PSR) is asymptotically optimal for expected social welfare among all social choice functions and we characterize this rule for a broad class of utility distributions. We further show that, among randomized PSRs, plurality uniquely maximizes expected social welfare for all power means. Experimentally, we find that optimal score vectors often yield substantially higher welfare than canonical score vectors. On highly structured utility distributions, optimal score vectors take on novel shapes unlike existing canonical score vectors, highlighting open questions for future analysis.
